repos.title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
repos.paper_summary:
Any3R is a feed-forward model that reconstructs scene geometry and camera poses from images taken by any mix of central cameras, including pinhole, fisheye and panoramic lenses, with no calibration search, undistortion or per-lens retraining. It changes two parts of a geometry foundation model that assume pinhole images. Angular coordinates replace the pixel-index rotary positional encoding with each patch's ray angles, computed per view from the ray field (the unit ray through every pixel). Solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the sphere area each pixel covers. Training uses panoramas and views resampled through eight central camera models.

Evaluation covers 13 central camera models across Matterport3D, Stanford2D3DS and PanoCity, with each method using its own predicted poses. Accuracy is the mean distance from reconstructed points to the nearest ground-truth point. On indoor equirectangular views, Any3R reaches 0.054 m versus 0.072 m for PanoVGGT. On outdoor equirectangular views it reaches 0.663 m versus 0.751 m for PanoVGGT. On indoor 90° pinhole views it reaches 0.076 m versus 0.092 m for MapAnything with the true ray field.

Limitations: the margin over pinhole baselines is smallest at 90°, and the method covers central cameras only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Pinhole-only geometry models cannot mix wide and panoramic cameras, and Any3R addresses this with per-pixel ray directions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior feed-forward models assume pinhole input, and camera-specific methods each fix one projection, so a change of lens means a change of model.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Any3R feeds each view's ray field into the rotary encoding and a solid-angle weight into the point loss, so no lens parameters are needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On indoor scenes, Any3R has the lowest Acc on all eight training cameras, from 0.052 m to 0.091 m.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: One feed-forward model reconstructs any central camera mix, evaluated on thirteen camera models across three datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists evaluation protocol, per-dataset and per-camera tables, zero-shot fisheye setup, and the rotary-frequency split ablation.

repos.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
repos.paper_summary: LongBanana is a benchmark of 90 expert-designed, expert-verified tasks for synthesizing one image from many reference images, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. Tasks average about 32 references and include hard-negative references that must be excluded. Each task is converted into an entity–relation graph, and items are scored on Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction by LongBananaEval, an agentic judge that calls tools such as OCR and counting. Reviewers labeled 46,700 item judgments; a 15% double-labeled subset reached 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. On output-level Overall scores, LongBananaEval reaches Pearson 0.8707, versus 0.8413 for a single-pass VLM judge. For generation, the paper compares direct prompting, agent harnesses, and RPR workflows, with Nano Banana 2 as the image generator. The best system, OpenClaw + RPR, scores 78.4 average and 47.8 P@70%, against 74.6 and 35.6 for PD-Direct, a baseline given the construction graph. RPR gains depend on the harness, and the paper notes it can introduce drift.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-reference image generation errors are provenance failures that holistic realism scores cannot localize.

digest_headlines.heading: The LongBanana Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: LongBanana contains 90 cases across a 3-by-3 taxonomy, each scored through atomic graph-derived checklist items.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Nano Banana 2 under OpenClaw with RPR scores 78.4 overall, above the 68.4 of full-prompt direct generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agentic workflows reach broader success than a fixed privileged schedule, and checklist scores localize failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from two Guangdong programs and KlingAI Research, and the authors declare no other competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, benchmark construction details, scorer and label quality statistics, extra experiments, and release safeguards.

repos.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
repos.paper_summary:
Unified training treats pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning, and suitable RL objectives as one maximum-likelihood objective over a changing mixture of static data and model-generated data. The paper implements this in a single trainer that mixes both sources. RL generations are weighted by 1/p̂ for each correct completion among N samples per prompt, and generation and training run asynchronously.

The evidence comes from a 124M-parameter model trained from scratch on a 20B-token pretraining corpus and a 510M-token midtraining corpus, using synthetic reasoning puzzles. Metrics are pass@1 accuracy and pass@16 coverage. The best unified configurations outperform staged training on held-out puzzles, including larger puzzles unseen in midtraining and RL. Under matched total compute, unified training reaches higher accuracy at larger budgets, while staged training is more compute-optimal for coverage.

Stated limitations: the experiments are small scale, no universally preferred mixture or schedule was found, no predictive scaling laws were established, and most runs optimize one RL task. The authors describe their continual-learning evidence as initial.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Foundation-model training stages can be unified under one likelihood objective, with data mixture as the main design choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Maximum-likelihood loss and the expected-reward policy gradient are set out as the two starting objectives.

digest_headlines.heading: A Unified Likelihood View of Foundation-Model Training
digest_headlines.headline: RL objectives reduce to maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated targets, so static and generated data share one loss.

digest_headlines.heading: Practical Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: A shared buffer, one token-weighted loss, and asynchronous generation implement the unified trainer.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: In controlled reasoning tasks unified training gains accuracy and generalization, while compute-optimality depends on budget and metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans foundation-model training pipelines, hybrid offline and online RL, and reward-guided self-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Open questions remain on choosing mixtures and schedules, scaling, optimization, multi-task training, and larger scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers data-mixing and compute conventions, loss normalization, derivations for policy-gradient baselines and continuous rewards, and supplementary results.

repos.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: Hexels are planar hexagonal surface elements, each with a soft hexagonal support and a first-order RGB color field over local coordinates. The method targets view synthesis, surface reconstruction, and 2D image fitting. Each primitive is evaluated at perspective-correct ray-plane intersections and composited in depth order, as in 2DGS. The base variant uses 20 learned parameters per primitive, versus 58 for 2DGS. Across 34 real scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB, with up to 3.6× lower peak training VRAM. On 15 DTU scans, mean Chamfer distance is 0.978 mm versus 1.375 mm for 2DGS. On six Tanks and Temples surface scenes, mean F1 is 34.38% versus 31.72%. On the 45-image Image-GS benchmark, PSNR rises from 33.16 to 35.82 dB. Limitations: a first-order color model cannot represent high-frequency texture within one primitive, sparse initialization can leave regions uncovered, the surfaces do not form a watertight mesh, and Hexels do not win every metric against every baseline. The primitives are planar only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing surface primitives need many overlapping elements for smooth regions, so this paper proposes one hexagonal primitive with a first-order color field.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods add memory through heavier kernels, textures, or neural fields, so this paper redesigns the primitive itself.

digest_headlines.heading: Hexels: Hexagonal Surface Elements
digest_headlines.headline: A Hexel pairs a soft hexagonal support with a linear color field, using 20 learned parameters in its view-independent form.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 34 scenes, Hexels reach higher PSNR than 2DGS at matched memory and at matched primitive budgets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Hexels establish a quality–efficiency frontier among evaluated surface primitives, but a first-order color cannot model arbitrary texture.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers parameterization, derivatives, rasterization, compression, and per-scene and qualitative results.

repos.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
repos.paper_summary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative drift in multi-turn image editing by steering only the late denoising steps of a base editor. The refined model is trained on its own on-policy rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Early steps are trained to match the frozen base model's velocity. Later steps blend that velocity with a preservation velocity toward a source-based endpoint, with the blend weight falling from 1 at the steering onset to 0 at the final step. The method is tested on FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT, and Qwen-Image-2.1. The paper reports substantially reduced drift over 15 to 20 editing turns. On FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, Qwen-IB EN changes by at most +0.47 across the tested steering onsets. Limitations: drift is measured only over 15 to 20 turns, training uses only identity and local edit families, and qualitative comparisons use one steering onset.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.

repos.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
repos.paper_summary: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness, Tilapia, for having AI agents build machine-checked TLA+ proofs of properties of real-world system specifications using the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS). The benchmark has 265 proof targets from 95 specifications; the evaluation uses an active set of 70 targets across 12 specifications. Tilapia gives agents TLAPS, the SANY parser, the TLC and Apalache model checkers, and proof libraries. It accepts a proof only if the target statement and specification are unchanged, every lemma the target transitively depends on is proved, and the proof passes grading in a fresh container with the original tools. The highest-scoring configuration, GPT-6.1 Sol (Codex) at max effort, proved 31 of 70 targets (44.3%, pass@3), at a total cost of USD 328.86. Other configurations scored 34.3% to 42.9%. The agents proved properties for specifications such as Bosco, the German protocol, and several write-ahead logs. The authors report 46 specification issues found during task construction, 35 of which were fixed. Limitations: the evaluation covers only 70 targets and two frontier model families; the paper reports that naive calls to automated backends are ineffective, and that invariant choice strongly affects proof difficulty.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: TLAPS-Bench tests whether AI agents can build end-to-end machine-checked TLA+ proofs for real-world system specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: TLA+ theorems are accepted only when TLAPS verifies the proof, while model checkers help test candidate invariants.

digest_headlines.heading: Tilapia: TLA+ Proof Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Tilapia gives agents proof tools and blocks cheating by making targets read-only and grading in a clean container.

digest_headlines.heading: TLAPS-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark holds 95 specifications and 265 targets, and evaluation uses an active set of 70 targets from 12 specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort proved 31 of 70 targets (44.3%), and all models failed on Wildfire refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks mostly supply proof structure, and the closest TLA+ benchmark supplies inductive invariants to agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Abstraction and refinement across layers are expected to scale proofs, as AI lowers the cost of formal proofs.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the retired problem set, per-target results, specification fixes with counterexamples, and the agent prompt and skills.

repos.title: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration
repos.paper_summary:
TaoMate-FVSR is an audio-guided facial video restoration framework for AI-generated video that also supports dubbing under replacement audio. It is a reference-guided flow model built on a Wan video DiT. Reconstruction starts from a mix of the source latent and Gaussian noise (strength 0.80 to 0.95), so the source mouth is not a fixed target. Reference frames and a four-frame motion history enter separate temporal slots. Training has two stages: visual restoration on degraded images and videos, then lip correction on degraded dubbed sources conditioned on target audio, with a SyncNet loss.

On a 150-video talking-head benchmark at 4× downsampling, it reports LPIPS 0.0793 and DISTS 0.0858, versus 0.1380 and 0.1421 for InstantRestore, and Sync-C/Sync-D of 7.413/7.561, versus 6.545/8.170 for SparkVSR. SparkVSR has higher PSNR (30.62 vs 28.67 dB) and SSIM (0.8863 vs 0.8836). On 30 replacement-audio clips, the enhanced-reference variant reaches Sync-C 8.175, versus 7.917 for the best cascade.

Limitations: the main comparison uses the ground-truth first frame as reference, and the enhanced-reference variant lowers PSNR to 23.52 dB. Native AIGC results are qualitative only.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Restoring small AIGC faces requires lip and teeth detail that agrees with the spoken audio, not only sharper pixels.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans facial and video restoration, generative restoration, visual dubbing, and audio-assisted restoration; the authors focus on unreliable mouths.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method mixes source latents with noise to start flow reconstruction and injects sparse references and history into separate temporal slots.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 150-video benchmark, Ours has the lowest paired perceptual error, while SparkVSR leads pixel-level fidelity.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors state that reconstructed facial detail is a generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance, and raise impersonation risk.

repos.title: RoboAtom: Large-scale Atomic-Action Supervision for Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary: RoboAtom introduces RoboAtom-Data, a set of 1,446,974 robot trajectories from 16 sources with time-aligned atomic-action annotations (6,876,282 skill-labeled segments, 16,882.1 hours), built with human seed annotation, PhysExtend, and quality control. PhysExtend propagates boundaries from a few same-task reference trajectories by dynamic programming over skill-specific physical cues (gripper state, motion intensity, pauses) and monotonic projection. On a 100-task extension set, PhysExtend reaches 71.0 Skill F1@0.7 with one reference, versus 48.5 for Cortex, and 69% episode accuracy versus 37% for Cortex; at 2.8×10⁻⁵ USD per source-video hour, versus about 100 USD for manual annotation. The paper also presents RoboAtom-Bench (500 expert-reviewed trajectories, 4,018 GT segments) and RoboAtom-Anno, a model trained on the annotations that the authors report outperforms all evaluated open- and closed-source models on RoboAtom-Bench and WGO-Bench. Reference models recover skill order (GPT-5.6-sol scores 63.4 Edit) but miss precise boundaries (28.0 temporal F1@0.7), and segment counts diverge on long trajectories. Downstream, atomic-action supervision with hierarchical execution is reported to improve task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. Limitations: the policy-pretraining effect is not verified, and egocentric human video is not included, with brief human actions hard to localize at the current sampling rate.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RoboAtom-Data adds time-aligned atomic-action labels to 1.45 million trajectories from 16 sources.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior subtask-annotated datasets use inconsistent vocabularies and granularity, and reference-based boundary propagation can struggle with variable execution speed.

digest_headlines.heading: RoboAtom-Data
digest_headlines.headline: Seed annotations are propagated to same-task trajectories with PhysExtend and released only after 85% segmentation and 75% episode accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: RoboAtom-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Reference models recover skill order but miss boundaries: GPT-5.6-sol reaches 63.4 Edit but only 28.0 temporal F1@0.7.

digest_headlines.heading: Learning with Atomic-Action Supervision
digest_headlines.headline: RoboAtom-Anno-9B outperforms all evaluated reference models on RoboAtom-Bench, and atomic-action control reaches 98.20% on LIBERO-Long.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Atomic-action supervision has not been tested in large-scale policy pretraining, and egocentric human video is not yet included.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion reports that RoboAtom-Anno beats evaluated models on annotation and that atomic supervision improves control over task-level baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists annotation prompts, per-source statistics, skill vocabulary, source mapping rules, training data, cost accounting, and image augmentation controls.

repos.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
repos.paper_summary: ToolSpace is a tool-centric framework for synthesizing verifiable, long-horizon agent training tasks from real tool-call traces rather than from synthesized databases. It mines data, state, and retry dependencies between adjacent calls with deterministic rules, clusters the resulting weighted graph into 804 environments, and creates databases only for state-mutating environments. State-aware random walks with rollback build chains, which are decompiled into natural-language tasks with assertion-based checks and kept only if they replay from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and τ3-Bench Banking, the Pro versions are harder: seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6. The paper reports that execution-witnessed edges outperform LLM-judged ones in ablations and that performance improves with data and environment scale. The graph has 77,760 nodes, and edges are 69% data, 25% state, and 6% retry. Limitations: the paper's real-trace sources are weighted toward synthetic-tool data for some groups, and the Pro benchmarks are constructed by the same pipeline, so their difficulty reflects the method's own construction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Data-centric synthesis derives tools after databases, so tool interfaces may not match real services; ToolSpace starts from execution traces instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior environment scaling fixes tool composition before drawing tasks, whereas ToolSpace composes tools from observed executions.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Tool-centric synthesis requires walks on a typed graph whose chains replay from the initial state.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Deterministic rules build the tool graph, and only walks that replay from the initial state become training data.

digest_headlines.heading: AutomationBench Pro and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking Pro
digest_headlines.headline: Expert-reviewed Pro versions of two benchmarks, with 300 and 98 tasks, require more tool calls than standard splits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: ToolSpace lifts Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6 across seven benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Conclusion restates that replay-verified, execution-witnessed composition drives gains and scales with data and environments.

repos.title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
repos.paper_summary:
BrickWright is a framework that lets pre-trained LLM agents generate physically feasible LEGO brick builds from text or image prompts by writing code against BrickLayer, a Python package for part search, assembly, and validation. The agent works in a plan-execute-validate loop: it writes `build.py`, runs a validator that checks for collisions and floating parts alongside agent-written tests, and finalizes once the checks pass. BrickLayer's assembly API mates connectors and snaps parts to a grid. The paper reports that it roughly halves inference cost compared with raw LDraw.

On 512 prompts from BrickNet-512, BrickWright-guided agents reach 100% validity for every tested model. Unguided GPT-6 Luna reaches 0.086 validity. VQAScore prompt adherence rises from 0.6504 to 0.6945 for Luna and from 0.6032 to 0.6523 for Haiku 5.5. Specialized models score 0.318 validity (BrickNet) and 0.990 validity (BrickGPT). Without the validator, all agents score below 79% validity.

Limitations: the feasibility definition excludes stability and assembly sequences. Agentic methods are slower than specialized models; BrickNet takes 5s per prompt, while full BrickWright takes 143s to 415s.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents often produce invalid brick assemblies, so this paper proposes a toolkit with an assembly API and a validator.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior brick generation relies on small vocabularies or fixed templates, while agentic 3D tools do not consider physical constraints.

digest_headlines.heading: BrickWright
digest_headlines.headline: BrickWright has an agent write Python build code with BrickLayer, validating collisions, floaters, and connectivity in a plan-execute-validate loop.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: BrickWright raises validity to 100% on 512 prompts, with Luna rising from 9% to 100% and prompt adherence held or improved.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Lightweight agents reach 100% validity, but feasibility excludes stability and assembly sequences, and agents run slower and costlier.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists valid@k results, validation failure breakdowns, prompts, the system prompt and API reference, and vanilla agent analysis.
